title: OpenAI retires o3 from ChatGPT after 90-day sunset, routes users to GPT-5
subtitle: The reasoning model that anchored ChatGPT's advanced tier for a year is now gone from the consumer product — API access continues until December.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: OpenAI removed the o3 model family from ChatGPT today, closing a 90-day sunset window that began with a May 28 deprecation notice. Existing ChatGPT conversations that were running on o3 or o3-pro automatically continue on the corresponding GPT-5 model, and the model picker no longer offers o3 as a choice. The o3-mini variant follows on October 1, with o4-mini as its replacement. Access through the API remains live until December 11, when o3 will be replaced by gpt-5.6-sol.

The retirement is significant because o3 was, for much of the past year, the flagship reasoning model that defined what ChatGPT could do on hard problems — math, code, planning, multi-step research. Migrating it out of the consumer product is a bet that GPT-5's routing layer, which decides in real time how much compute to spend on a given query, now covers the same ground more efficiently. It also forces every enterprise that hard-coded o3 into an internal workflow to test their prompts and eval suites against a new model in the next three months.

This is part of a broader pattern of accelerated model consolidation across the frontier labs. GPT-4.5 was retired earlier this summer, o3-mini's sunset is scheduled for October, and Anthropic and Google have both narrowed their public model lineups over the same period. The industry that spent 2024 and early 2025 shipping new named checkpoints every few weeks is now trimming them just as quickly — partly to concentrate GPU capacity, partly because the newer generation has closed the gap on the specialized reasoning workloads that justified keeping older models around.

For learners: treat model deprecation as a normal, recurring event, not a surprise. If you build anything on a specific model version — a prompt library, a class assignment, a small side project — write down which model you tested it against, and re-run the eval every quarter. The skill that matters isn't picking the right model once; it's noticing when the ground shifts underneath and being ready to migrate without starting over.
